section_summary: This section contains State Department records filed under decimal file 894.403 (Fine Arts in Japan) spanning 1930 to 1937, consisting of despatches, letters, memoranda, telegrams, and cross-reference sheets. Early documents from 1930 focus on Count Makino's request through Ambassador William R. Castle, Jr. for information on the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts to guide municipal development and prevent eyesore monuments during the post-earthquake reconstruction of Tokyo. Later records document State Department introductions for the Misses Wyatt to study private Japanese art collections in 1937, extensive internal deliberations in 1935 regarding the proposed acquisition of Alexander G. Moslé's renowned collection of Japanese armor and sword furniture by the Smithsonian Institution, Japanese participation in the 1939 San Francisco Exposition art exhibit, and architectural studies by Mr. Boyce.

subfiles.about: Ambassador Castle reports that Count Makino requested full information on the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts to guide municipal development and prevent eyesore monuments in post-earthquake Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: American Ambassador William R. Castle, Jr. writes from Tokyo reporting a conversation with Count Makino, Lord Privy Seal of Japan, who inquired about the laws and regulations governing the Commission of Fine Arts in Washington and similar municipal planning bodies. Castle explains that the temporary reconstruction board in Tokyo lacks permanence and that schemes exist to erect undesirable monuments, causing distress to the Imperial Household. He recommends sending the despatch to Commission Chairman Charles Moore and suggests that Moore provide advice and a personal letter to assist the Japanese government.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 104 from Ambassador W. R. Castle, Jr., Regarding Japanese Interest in the Commission of Fine Arts

subfiles.about: The Department of State transmits Ambassador Castle's despatch to Fine Arts Commission Chairman Charles Moore, requesting information and advice for Count Makino.
subfiles.summary: Assistant Secretary of State Wilbur J. Carr transmits a copy of Ambassador Castle's despatch No. 104 to Charles Moore, Chairman of the Commission of Fine Arts. Carr explains Count Makino's request for information regarding the Commission and other municipal planning commissions in the United States. He notes Castle's suggestion that Moore write a personal letter offering advice from his wide experience and requests that any reply be sent care of the Department, as Castle may have already departed Tokyo for Washington.
subfiles.title: Letter from Department of State to Charles Moore Transmitting Ambassador Castle's Despatch

subfiles.about: The Department of State informs Ambassador Castle that his request concerning the Fine Arts Commission has been forwarded to Chairman Charles Moore.
subfiles.summary: Assistant Secretary of State Wilbur J. Carr acknowledges Ambassador Castle's despatch No. 104 and encloses a copy of the Department's letter to Charles Moore, Chairman of the Commission of Fine Arts. Carr assures Castle that as soon as Mr. Moore's reply is received, it will be communicated to him.
subfiles.title: Instruction from Department of State to Ambassador W. R. Castle, Jr.

subfiles.about: Fine Arts Commission Chairman Charles Moore agrees to confer with Ambassador Castle upon his return to Washington regarding assistance to the Japanese Government.
subfiles.summary: Charles Moore, Chairman of the Commission of Fine Arts, acknowledges receipt of Assistant Secretary Carr's letter of May 16 and Ambassador Castle's despatch of April 18. Moore states that when Castle returns to Washington, he will discuss with him an appropriate response and guidance to be provided to the Japanese Government.
subfiles.title: Letter from Charles Moore to Assistant Secretary of State Wilbur J. Carr

subfiles.about: A cross-reference note recording a letter to the Treasury Department regarding a two-volume catalog of Japanese art addressed to Dr. Hornbeck.
subfiles.summary: This Document File Note cross-references a letter dated September 16, 1935, to the Treasury Department filed under 093.941/76a. It concerns a two-volume catalog depicting a collection of Japanese objets d'art addressed to Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck, who suggested it might be acquired by the Department for deposit in the Library or the Archives.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Two-Volume Catalog of Japanese Objets d'Art

subfiles.about: Walter Lichtenstein requests State Department assistance and introductions for the Misses Wyatt to view private art collections in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Walter Lichtenstein, Vice President of the First National Bank of Chicago, writes to Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck on behalf of his bank president's sisters-in-law, the Misses Wyatt, including author Edith Wyatt. He explains that the ladies are sailing on August 5 for several months in Japan to study Oriental art and wish to view private collections in Tokyo, notably that of Baron Yanosuke Iwasaki. Lichtenstein asks whether these collections are open to the public and requests introductions to facilitate their visit, noting also that historian Bernadotte Schmitt is recovering well from an operation.
subfiles.title: Letter from Walter Lichtenstein to Stanley K. Hornbeck Regarding the Misses Wyatt

subfiles.about: Dr. Hornbeck writes Ambassador Grew requesting assistance for the Misses Wyatt during their visit to private art collections in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck informs Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo of a request from Walter Lichtenstein on behalf of the Misses Wyatt, sisters-in-law of Chicago bank president Edward Eagle Brown. He notes that the ladies have literary distinction and wish to see the private art collections of Baron Iwasaki and others. Hornbeck encloses a letter of introduction and asks Grew to render any possible assistance.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew

subfiles.about: Dr. Hornbeck encloses a letter of introduction for the Misses Wyatt to Ambassador Grew and suggests contacting Count Kabayama in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck responds to Walter Lichtenstein's inquiry regarding the Misses Wyatt's upcoming trip to Japan. Hornbeck explains that while he cannot state whether private collections like Baron Iwasaki's have regular public visiting days, serious students are usually welcomed if properly introduced. He encloses a letter of introduction to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew, recommending that Grew introduce the visitors to Count Kabayama of Kokusai Bunka Shinkokai, and expresses pleasure at Bernadotte Schmitt's recovery.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Walter Lichtenstein

subfiles.about: A formal letter of introduction for the Misses Wyatt addressed to Ambassador Grew, suggesting Count Kabayama facilitate access to art collections.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck provides a letter of introduction for the Misses Wyatt of Chicago, who are traveling to Japan to study Oriental art and visit private collections such as that of Baron Iwasaki. Hornbeck suggests that Ambassador Grew introduce them to Count Kabayama through his position with the Kokusai Bunka Shinko Kai, or to another suitable person who can arrange permits to view private and official collections.
subfiles.title: Letter of Introduction for the Misses Wyatt Addressed to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew

subfiles.about: Edith F. Wyatt asks Dr. Hornbeck whether they should proceed with or cancel their sailing to Japan in light of current conditions.
subfiles.summary: Edith F. Wyatt telegraphs Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck from Chicago thanking him for his letter to Walter Lichtenstein. She states that they have booked passage to Japan on the Asama Maru sailing from San Francisco on August 5 for a four-month art study trip. In light of prevailing political and military conditions, she urgently requests telegraphic advice on whether to continue their plans or cancel their sailing.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Edith F. Wyatt to Stanley K. Hornbeck Inquiring About Travel to Japan

subfiles.about: Dr. Hornbeck advises Edith F. Wyatt that the State Department is not advising against travel to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck sends a telegraphic response via Western Union to Miss Edith F. Wyatt in Chicago. He informs her that on the basis of present information available to the Department of State, the Department is not advising against travel to Japan.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Edith F. Wyatt Regarding Travel Advice

subfiles.about: Walter Lichtenstein thanks Dr. Hornbeck for the letter of introduction provided to the Misses Wyatt.
subfiles.summary: Walter Lichtenstein writes to Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck expressing sincere gratitude for his letter and the enclosed introduction to Ambassador Grew on behalf of the Misses Wyatt. He notes that the assistance is deeply appreciated by himself, bank president Edward E. Brown, and Brown's sisters-in-law. Lichtenstein adds that Bernadotte Schmitt sends warm regards and is recovering well.
subfiles.title: Letter from Walter Lichtenstein to Stanley K. Hornbeck Expressing Gratitude

subfiles.about: A cross-reference note regarding discussions with Langdon Warner on securing Japanese cooperation for an art exhibit at the 1939 San Francisco Exposition.
subfiles.summary: This Document File Note cross-references an October 1937 memorandum by Joseph W. Ballantine filed under 811.607-San Francisco 1939/202. The memorandum records the substance of a conversation between Langdon Warner of the Fogg Art Museum and State Department officials regarding Warner's request for Department assistance in obtaining Japanese cooperation for an art exhibit at the 1939 San Francisco Exposition.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Langdon Warner Conference on San Francisco Exposition Art Exhibit

subfiles.about: Mabel T. Boardman recommends that the Secretary of State explore acquiring Alexander Moslé's collection of Japanese arms and armor for the Smithsonian Institution.
subfiles.summary: Mabel T. Boardman writes to Stanley K. Hornbeck bringing attention to a very large and fine collection of Japanese art formed by former Belgian Consul Alexander Moslé during his twelve years in Japan. She notes that the collection is especially rich in arms and armor from prehistoric times to the abolition of swords, as well as lacquer, textiles, paintings, and pottery. Boardman urges that the collection be secured for the United States Government under the Smithsonian Institution, noting that Frederic A. Delano is interested and suggesting that Hornbeck confer with Moslé and inform the Secretary of State.
subfiles.title: Letter from Mabel T. Boardman to Stanley K. Hornbeck Proposing Acquisition of the Moslé Collection

subfiles.about: Dr. Hornbeck reluctantly declines to recommend Secretary of State intervention in acquiring the Moslé collection for the Smithsonian.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck replies to Mabel T. Boardman's letter of February 11 regarding Alexander Moslé's Japanese art collection. He encloses a copy of his letter to Moslé and states that after consulting experts, he must reluctantly abstain from enlisting the Secretary of State's interest in having the Smithsonian Institution acquire the collection. He suggests Boardman inform Moslé that competent authorities consider the National Museum the most suitable repository in Washington for his collection of armor and sword furniture.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Mabel T. Boardman Regarding the Moslé Collection (File Carbon)

subfiles.about: Department letterhead copy of Dr. Hornbeck's letter to Mabel T. Boardman regarding the Moslé collection.
subfiles.summary: This is a Department of State letterhead copy of Stanley K. Hornbeck's letter of March 6, 1935, to Mabel T. Boardman. Hornbeck informs Boardman that he cannot urge the Secretary of State to pursue Smithsonian acquisition of Alexander Moslé's Japanese art collection. He suggests that the National Museum would be the most suitable repository in Washington for the collection of armor and sword furniture.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Mabel T. Boardman Regarding the Moslé Collection (Letterhead Copy)

subfiles.about: Dr. Hornbeck explains the administrative governance of the Smithsonian Institution and declines to urge State Department intervention in purchasing Moslé's collection.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck writes to Alexander G. Moslé acknowledging his letter of February 18 and expressing gratitude for the gift of Volumes I and II of the printed catalog of his collection. Hornbeck explains that while having such a high-quality collection in Washington would offer many advantages, object acquisitions fall exclusively under the Smithsonian Regents rather than the Establishment, which has never convened in the institution's history. Consequently, Hornbeck states he must abstain from urging the Secretary of State to initiate purchase proceedings and requests instructions on the disposal of papers and a portfolio left by Moslé.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Alexander G. Moslé Regarding Proposed Smithsonian Acquisition

subfiles.about: Additional carbon copy of Dr. Hornbeck's March 6, 1935 letter to Mabel T. Boardman regarding the Moslé collection.
subfiles.summary: An additional file carbon copy of the March 6, 1935 letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Miss Mabel T. Boardman. The letter communicates Hornbeck's decision not to involve the Secretary of State in purchasing Alexander Moslé's collection of Japanese armor and sword furniture for the Smithsonian Institution, suggesting the National Museum instead.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Mabel T. Boardman (Carbon Copy)

subfiles.about: Faint carbon copy of Dr. Hornbeck's March 6, 1935 letter to Mabel T. Boardman.
subfiles.summary: A faint duplicate carbon copy of Stanley K. Hornbeck's letter dated March 6, 1935, to Mabel T. Boardman. The letter declines to recommend the purchase of the Moslé Japanese art collection by the Smithsonian Institution through the Secretary of State and suggests the National Museum as a more appropriate repository.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Mabel T. Boardman (Faint Carbon Copy)

subfiles.about: An internal filing slip marked with decimal file number 894.403.
subfiles.summary: A departmental slip or wrapper bearing fragmentary notations and the decimal file classification number 894.403. It served as an internal filing separation or marker within the Moslé collection correspondence dossier.
subfiles.title: Filing Slip for Decimal File 894.403

subfiles.about: Dr. Hornbeck agrees to meet Alexander G. Moslé in Washington on Saturday morning, February 16, 1935.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck replies to Alexander G. Moslé's letter of February 12, agreeing to meet him on Saturday morning, February 16. Hornbeck suggests that Moslé telephone his State Department office upon arriving in Washington to arrange a mutually convenient hour for their conference.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Alexander G. Moslé Scheduling an Appointment

subfiles.about: Calling card / address slip of Alexander G. Moslé showing his New York address.
subfiles.summary: An address slip or calling card of Alexander G. Moslé showing his residence at 5 East Sixty-sixth Street, New York, with notations referencing Dr. Hornbeck and decimal file number 894.403. It was retained in the Department files in connection with Moslé's visits to Washington.
subfiles.title: Calling Card of Alexander G. Moslé

subfiles.about: An office message slip recording an appointment for Dr. Hornbeck to see Alexander G. Moslé at 10:00 AM on February 16, 1935.
subfiles.summary: A Department of State internal telephone or reception message slip dated February 16, 1935, at 9:05 AM. It notifies Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck ('SKH') that a visitor (Alexander G. Moslé) is scheduled to see him at 10:00 AM that day.
subfiles.title: Office Message Slip Regarding Appointment with Alexander G. Moslé

subfiles.about: Eugene H. Dooman reports expert appraisals of the Moslé collection and advises against involving the Secretary of State in Smithsonian acquisition.
subfiles.summary: Eugene H. Dooman of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs reports on his discussions with John Ellerton Lodge of the Freer Gallery and an American Oriental art dealer regarding the Moslé collection. Both experts praised the collection as probably the finest of its kind in the United States and equal to Europe's best. However, Lodge explained the administrative structure of the Smithsonian Institution and advised that it would be unwise for the Secretary of State to become involved. Dooman attaches draft letters to Moslé and Boardman and suggests briefing the Secretary briefly.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Eugene H. Dooman on the Moslé Collection of Japanese Armor and Sword Furniture

subfiles.about: A cross-reference note recording personal letters sent by Dr. Hornbeck to Alexander G. Moslé and Mabel T. Boardman.
subfiles.summary: A Document File Note dated March 6, 1935, recording personal letters from Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck to Mr. Alexander G. Moslé and Miss Mabel T. Boardman. The note documents that both letters relate to the proposed acquisition and handling of the Moslé collection of Japanese art.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Recording Letters to Alexander G. Moslé and Mabel T. Boardman

subfiles.about: Carbon copy of Dr. Hornbeck's letter explaining why the Secretary of State cannot initiate Smithsonian purchase of Moslé's collection.
subfiles.summary: A two-page file carbon copy of the letter dated March 6, 1935, from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Alexander G. Moslé. Hornbeck thanks Moslé for the two catalog volumes and explains that Smithsonian acquisition policies rest with its Regents rather than the Establishment. He states he cannot urge the Secretary of State to take action and asks for instructions regarding the return or disposal of Moslé's papers and portfolio.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Alexander G. Moslé (Carbon Copy)

subfiles.about: Department letterhead copy of Dr. Hornbeck's letter to Alexander G. Moslé regarding the Smithsonian Institution.
subfiles.summary: A two-page Department of State letterhead copy of Stanley K. Hornbeck's letter to Alexander G. Moslé dated March 6, 1935. Hornbeck expresses appreciation for Moslé's collection catalog but explains that the statutory Establishment of the Smithsonian Institution does not handle acquisitions, precluding intervention by the Secretary of State.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Alexander G. Moslé (Letterhead Copy)

subfiles.about: A handwritten slip from Alexander G. Moslé requesting to call on Dr. Hornbeck to discuss his collection.
subfiles.summary: A short handwritten note from Alexander G. Moslé asking if he may call on Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck in Washington to talk further regarding his collection and papers. The note is marked with decimal file number 894.403.
subfiles.title: Handwritten Message from Alexander G. Moslé Requesting an Appointment

subfiles.about: Maxwell M. Hamilton acknowledges Moslé's letter and schedules a tentative meeting with Dr. Hornbeck for March 23, 1935.
subfiles.summary: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Assistant Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, acknowledges Alexander G. Moslé's letter of March 19 during Dr. Hornbeck's absence in New York. Hamilton arranges a tentative appointment for Moslé to meet Hornbeck at his State Department office on Saturday morning, March 23, at 11:00 AM, requesting confirmation by telephone.
subfiles.title: Letter from Maxwell M. Hamilton to Alexander G. Moslé Scheduling an Appointment

subfiles.about: Additional carbon copy of Dr. Hornbeck's March 6, 1935 letter declining to seek Smithsonian purchase of the Moslé collection.
subfiles.summary: An additional two-page carbon copy of Stanley K. Hornbeck's letter of March 6, 1935, to Alexander G. Moslé. The letter conveys the Department's position that acquisitions by the Smithsonian Institution are the exclusive domain of its Regents and declines secretarial intervention.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Alexander G. Moslé (Additional Carbon Copy)

subfiles.about: Carbon copy of Eugene H. Dooman's memorandum summarizing appraisals of the Moslé collection and advising against secretarial involvement.
subfiles.summary: A carbon copy of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum dated March 6, 1935, by Eugene H. Dooman. It summarizes consultations with John Ellerton Lodge of the Freer Gallery and an art dealer regarding the exceptional quality of Alexander Moslé's collection of Japanese armor and sword furniture, while reiterating that the Secretary of State should not become involved.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Eugene H. Dooman on the Moslé Collection (Carbon Copy)

subfiles.about: Further duplicate carbon copy of Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck's letter to Alexander G. Moslé dated March 6, 1935.
subfiles.summary: A further duplicate two-page carbon copy of Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck's letter to Alexander G. Moslé dated March 6, 1935. It explains the governance rules of the Smithsonian Institution and declines to urge secretarial action for acquiring the collection.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Alexander G. Moslé (Duplicate Carbon Copy)

subfiles.about: Further duplicate carbon copy of Dr. Hornbeck's March 6, 1935 letter to Mabel T. Boardman.
subfiles.summary: A further duplicate carbon copy of Stanley K. Hornbeck's letter of March 6, 1935, to Mabel T. Boardman. The letter reports that after consultation with museum authorities, Hornbeck decided not to request Secretary of State intervention in acquiring Moslé's Japanese art collection for the Smithsonian Institution.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Mabel T. Boardman (Further Carbon Copy)

subfiles.about: W. T. Turner recommends filing papers without action regarding architectural and inventive studies in Japan by Mr. Boyce.
subfiles.summary: W. T. Turner of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs writes a memorandum regarding a proposed instruction concerning studies of Japanese inventive activities and the American Institute of Architects. Turner notes the difficulties of gathering material in the United States and suggests that while Mr. Boyce should confine his research to materials available in Japan, sending an instruction might discourage him from seeking other sources. He concludes that the best course is to file the appended correspondence without action and allow Mr. Boyce to conduct his architectural studies independently.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by W. T. Turner Regarding Studies on Japanese Architecture and Inventive Activities by Mr. Boyce
